cim: Google.org grants Clalit $2M for voice AI in healthcare
cim_eredeti: Google.org grants Clalit $2M for voice AI in healthcare
szoveg_eredeti:
Google.org has awarded Clalit Health Services a $2 million grant to develop a voice-driven AI assistant for Israeli healthcare.

The philanthropic arm of Google is underwriting Clalit’s “Digital Front Door”, an intelligent conversational assistant designed to make healthcare services more accessible, particularly for patients from diverse communities. Clalit is Israel’s largest healthcare organisation. The grant runs for two years and covers development through launch.

Boaz Maoz, Managing Director of Google Cloud Israel, said: “AI has the potential to address some of the most significant barriers to accessing healthcare.”By implementing secure conversational AI tailored to local dialects and unique communication channels, Clalit is ensuring that the benefits of digital healthcare reach every community.

“We are proud to support this initiative through our cloud infrastructure and to help establish a scalable, replicable model that can enable equitable and inclusive healthcare around the world.”

Google Gemini and large language models supply the conversational intelligence, running on Google Cloud’s secure infrastructure. Clalit builds and operates the assistant; Google Cloud hosts and secures it. The arrangement adds a regulated healthcare workload to a platform whose past outages have drawn attention from UK banking regulators.

It’s conceived as an intelligent digital layer that accompanies patients across the entire healthcare journey, helping them understand their healthcare needs, prepare for medical appointments, and manage follow-up care in their native languages, with continuous, personalised support.

Israel’s diverse communities speak a wide range of languages and dialects; Clalit has committed to equitable healthcare services for all patients.

Traditional digital platforms depend on written, formal language. That requirement excludes people who primarily communicate through local spoken dialects, so independent online appointment booking rates remain low, according to the joint announcement. Speech recognition in the system is tuned to those dialects and their cultural nuances, letting patients complete intake, triage, and appointment booking in the language they actually speak.

Prof. Eytan Wirtheim, Director General of Clalit Health Services, said: “What makes Clalit a unique and leading healthcare organisation on the international stage is the human mosaic and rich diversity of our patients.”

Interactive voice-based AI is integrated directly into landlines and standard mobile phones, the devices patients already use. The approach bypasses communication barriers altogether. Patients without internet connectivity, without a smartphone, or on devices that restrict access to standard web applications and SMS aren’t locked out, because the voice channel doesn’t need a data connection.

The tailored outreach is designed to increase enrolment in digital services and improve pre-appointment confirmations across a broader range of communities.

Clalit operates a zero-trust security framework with stringent data privacy measures for the deployment. Every patient interaction with the conversational AI is encrypted, stripped of personally identifiable information, and fully anonymised. The framework governs the voice conversations that will run over the phone network.

Rollout follows two steps. An initial pilot precedes nationwide deployment. Clalit then plans to publish the voice AI architecture and its cultural adaptation frameworks as an open-source model for public healthcare, so other public health systems can replicate the approach.

“The model we are developing here in Israel is intended to eventually become an open-source architecture, available to healthcare organisations around the world, allowing them to replicate the model and help ensure accessible healthcare for everyone,” Wirtheim concludes.
